note: Applies the technology, organization and environment framework to GenAI adoption across 108 organisations.
title: Towards Adoption of Generative AI in Organizational Settings
explain_beginner: Before most companies had any real experience with tools like ChatGPT, this paper asked a forward looking question, what will actually determine which organizations adopt generative AI and which do not. At the time it was written, the author points out, there was essentially no existing research on what factors shape this specific decision for this specific technology, so the paper set out to fill that gap using established ideas from technology adoption research rather than starting from scratch. It combines three established theories, one that looks at whether a technology fits an organization's needs and resources, one that looks at pressure from regulators and industry norms, and one that looks at how new ideas spread through a population of adopters over time, and tests them using data collected from over a hundred organizations in India. It found that these combined factors meaningfully explain why some organizations move to adopt generative AI and others do not. It does not tell us whether adoption actually improves performance once it happens, since the study is about the decision to adopt, not the outcome of adopting, and it draws on organizations from one country at an early moment in the technology's rollout.
explain_business: The practical use of this paper for a manager or consultant is as an early checklist of what actually predicts whether an organization will adopt generative AI, drawn from combining technology fit, institutional pressure, and innovation diffusion factors rather than from opinion. Because the underlying sample is 108 organizations in India collected shortly after generative AI tools became widely known, a business elsewhere should treat the specific factor weightings as directional rather than as fixed rules that necessarily transfer to a different regulatory environment or market. The paper stops at explaining adoption, it does not measure whether the organizations that adopted actually saw better performance, meaning it explains why organizations start using the technology rather than whether that decision paid off financially, so it is useful for planning an adoption strategy or change management effort but not for justifying a return on investment. This is relevant right now to any organization still in the early adoption decision phase for generative AI tools, and it becomes less relevant, and other papers more relevant, once an organization has already adopted and wants to measure the performance effect rather than understand the decision to adopt.
explain_practitioner: The paper builds its model around three established theoretical lenses, the Technology-Organization-Environment framework, institutional theory, and diffusion of innovation theory, combined to explain the specific drivers behind organizational adoption of generative AI tools such as ChatGPT. Data was collected from 108 organizations in India, and the study analyzes which technological, organizational, and environmental factors, alongside institutional and diffusion related variables, significantly predict adoption intention or behavior. The contribution the author claims explicitly is that prior research had not yet examined the specific determinants of generative AI adoption in organizational settings, positioning this as an early empirical study on that question rather than a confirmation of previously known effects specific to this technology. As a survey based, cross sectional study of a specific national sample, the design carries the standard limitation that the identified factors and their relative importance may not hold in other regulatory or economic environments outside India, and the paper studies intention and adoption itself rather than what happens to organizational performance afterward, so it cannot be used on its own to argue that adoption pays off.
